 7  ABSTRACT


     In modern science, a deep chasm separates the law-bound physical realm from the purposeful realm of life and mind, leaving
    concepts like meaning and agency seemingly beyond the reach of fundamental theory.  Universal Evolutionary Object
    Theory (UEOT) is presented as a ﬁrst-principles framework to bridge this divide and reunify our understanding of matter and
    meaning under a single coherent paradigm.
    At its core, UEOT rests on two original postulates that redeﬁne objecthood and evolution. First, the Topological Ontology of
    Existence posits that every persistently existing entity—every object in the UEOT sense—owes its identity and persistence
     to at least one internal, self-maintaining feedback loop, termed an Ω-loop. This topological loop continually regenerates the
     object’s pattern, serving as the essence of its identity. Second, the Dual Drive of Evolution posits that all processes of
    change in an object are governed by a balanced interplay of two complementary drives: a physical efﬁciency drive (Π) that
    urges the object to maximize energy and material economy (minimizing “cost”), and an informational drive (Φ) that urges the
     object to reduce uncertainty (maximize knowledge gain and adaptive complexity).
    From these foundations, UEOT yields a uniﬁed explanatory framework of remarkable breadth. It shows how teleology (goal-
     directed behavior) can emerge naturally from underlying physical dynamics.  In particular, an object’s long-term evolution
 8   converges toward a stable optimum—its Global Optimal Attractor (GOA), where energy use is maximally efﬁcient and infor-
    mation fully integrated—while the instantaneous direction of change deﬁnes the Global Optimal Direction (GOD) that steers
    the system toward that attractor.  Teleological behavior (goal-directedness) thus emerges not as mysticism but as a natu-
      ral macro-scale consequence of these underlying variational drives.  Crucially, UEOT also provides a practical diagnostic
      toolkit to quantify how closely any system’s local behavior aligns with its global evolutionary trajectory, effectively allowing the
    “purposefulness” of complex systems to be measured.
    Rather than a ﬁnalized theory, UEOT is presented as an open-ended framework and research program—a foundational
     blueprint rather than a ﬁnished ediﬁce.   It offers a novel, axiomatic worldview grounded in topology and information that
    not only integrates physical law and biological evolution, but also encompasses consciousness, social dynamics, and even
     philosophical notions of value and purpose. We emphasize that while the core principles are precisely deﬁned, many details
    remain open for reﬁnement and empirical testing. In this manifesto, we articulate the UEOT paradigm, highlight its conceptual
     originality and unifying power, and outline how it can be further developed and validated. Ultimately, UEOT aspires to construct
    a uniﬁed scientiﬁc worldview that reintroduces meaning and purpose into our description of nature, laying a conceptual
    cornerstone for the future evolution of a truly uniﬁed science.

19 1 Introduction—The Quest for a Uniﬁed Science

20  1.1 The Great Divide: Matter, Mind, and Meaning
21  Since the scientiﬁc revolution, human knowledge has splintered into a multitude of specialized domains. Physics has unveiled
22  precise mathematical laws of matter and energy from the quantum scale to the cosmic. Biology has elucidated the logic of
23   life through evolutionary theory and genetics, while the social sciences have probed the complexities of human behavior and
24   societies. Yet amid these triumphs of specialization, a fundamental ﬁssure remains in the landscape of modern science. On
25  one side lies the physical world, governed by impersonal laws that offer no hint of purpose; on the other side lies the world
26  of life and mind, brimming with apparent agency, adaptiveness, and teleological qualities (intent, “purpose,” “meaning”) that
27  do not obviously emerge from physical ﬁrst principles. To this day, physics cannot fully explain how life arose from non-
28   living matter; biology cannot pinpoint the emergence of subjective consciousness; and no established science can quantify the
29   origins of meaning or value. This schism—reminiscent of C. P. Snow’s famous “two cultures” divide between scientiﬁc and
30  humanistic knowledge1—has become a profound obstacle to a truly uniﬁed understanding of reality. We are prompted to ask:
31  can we discover deeper ﬁrst principles that bridge mind and matter, reconciling the world of mechanisms with the world of
32  meanings?


33  1.2 From Systems Thinking to Information Physics: Intellectual Precursors
34  The desire to unify knowledge is not new. Over the past century, visionary thinkers have pursued integrative frameworks
35   to heal this divide. For instance, Ludwig von Bertalanffy’s General Systems Theory pioneered cross-domain principles like
36  feedback and homeostasis, suggesting abstract laws applicable to biology and beyond2. Norbert Wiener’s Cybernetics like-
37  wise emphasized control and communication in organisms and machines, framing life and mind in terms of information
38  ﬂows and feedback loops3. Around the same time, Erwin Schrödinger introduced the notion of life feeding on “negative
39  entropy” as a clue to life’s thermodynamic basis4, hinting at how living systems maintain order by exporting entropy. In the
40  1970s, Ilya Prigogine’s theory of dissipative structures showed how ordered complexity can spontaneously emerge in far-from-
41  equilibrium chemical systems5, thereby bridging physics and the origin of self-organizing order. And in the quantum realm,
42  John Wheeler’s famous “it from bit” hypothesis boldly suggested that information underlies physical reality at the deepest
43   level6, erasing the boundary between physics and information.
44     More recent efforts have continued this integrative thread.  In origin-of-life research, Stuart Kauffman proposed that
45   life may have begun as collectively autocatalytic sets of molecules that mutually sustain one another, forming self-producing
46  metabolic networks out of purely chemical reactions7. This idea of matter self-organizing into a self-sustaining system without
47  external guidance offered a plausible bridge between chemistry and biology. In cognitive and brain science, Karl Friston’s
48  Free Energy Principle has been advanced as a unifying account of action and perception, positing that living agents maintain
49   their order by minimizing an information-theoretic quantity (surprise or “free energy”) in interaction with the environment8.
50  The free-energy principle thus connects biological self-maintenance with principles of inference and information, hinting at a
51  deep unity between life’s physiology and mind’s perception.
52       Parallel efforts in fundamental physicssuch as string theory9,10 and loop quantum gravity11,12sought to unify forces and
53  spacetime, while complexity pioneers like Murray Gell-Mann13 and John H. Holland14 emphasized universal patterns across
54   nature, and physicist P. W. Anderson argued for emergent laws at higher levels of complexity15, while integrative philoso-
55  phers like Ken Wilber and renowned biologist Edward O. Wilson advocated a holistic synthesis of knowledge16,17. Each of
56  these and other efforts illuminated important pieces of the puzzle, laying groundwork for a more uniﬁed science. Feedback
57  loops, self-organization, information and thermodynamics—all have been shown to play roles across physics, life, and mind.
58  However, none of the existing frameworks has yet delivered a single ﬁrst-principles theory that seamlessly integrates physical
59  laws, the dynamics of complex systems, the processing of information, and the apparent purposiveness of life and mind. In
60   short, a comprehensive cross-domain theoretical framework—one that can accommodate concepts of purpose and meaning in
61   naturalistic terms—remains elusive.


62  1.3 Toward a New First-Principles Framework: UEOT’s Foundations and Aims
63  In response to this long-standing challenge, we propose Universal Evolutionary Object Theory (UEOT) as a new unifying
64  framework built on ﬁrst principles. UEOT rests on two fundamental postulates concerning the nature of existence and evolu-
65   tion, which in combination aim to bridge the gap between matter and meaning.

66  Postulate 1: Topological Nature of Existence (Ω-loop Ontology).  Every entity that stably exists—every object in UEOT
67  terms—owes its identity and persistence to at least one internal, self-sustaining closed causal loop within its structure. In other
68  words, a stable object is not merely a static collection of parts, but a topological feedback cycle that continually regenerates
69  and self-maintains the object’s pattern. We term each such self-maintaining cycle an Ω-loop. In essence, topology is identity:
70  an object’s essence lies in the pattern of connections that allows it to continuously re-create and uphold itself. If the Ω-loop

71   is disrupted, the object loses its coherence and ceases to persist—much as a living cell disintegrates if its metabolic network
 72   is broken. This principle echoes earlier notions of self-producing systems, such as the autopoiesis concept in theoretical
 73  biology which describes life as a network of processes that recursively produces and maintains itself18. UEOT’s ontology thus
 74  formalizes a general version of this idea: to be is to engage in a closed, self-referential cycle of activity. Moreover, the degree
 75  of an object’s openness or closure delineates a basic ontological distinction. Objects with essentially closed Ω-loops (e.g. an
 76  atom or a rock) can passively persist without actively taking in external resources, whereas objects with open Ω-loops (e.g.
 77  a cell or organism) must continually exchange matter and energy with their environment to sustain themselves. In this view,
 78  being is deﬁned by doing—by an internalized loop of causal activity that makes an object self-maintaining.

 79  Postulate 2: Dual Evolutionary Drive (Π/Φ Principle).  All processes of change in an object—its behaviors, growth, and
 80  evolution over time—are governed by an interplay of two complementary drives, one physical and one informational. This con-
 81   stitutes a universal variational principle for evolution, acting on the object’s state. On the one hand, there is a drive for physical
 82  efﬁcacy, denoted Π, which compels the system to use energy and material resources efﬁciently—seeking to minimize waste
 83  or “cost” while maximizing functional output. On the other hand, there is a drive for informational improvement, denoted
 84  Φ, which compels the system to acquire useful information, reduce uncertainty, and increase its organizational complexity or
 85  ﬁtness. In plain terms, Π is an efﬁciency/exploitation drive and Φ is an information/exploration drive. Nature, according to
 86  UEOT, never optimizes a single objective in isolation; every system is continually navigating a trade-off between these two
 87  fundamental incentives—between doing what works now versus learning what could work better later. The trajectory of a
 88  system’s evolution emerges from this dynamic tension between Π and Φ. This dual-drive formulation resonates with ideas
 89  across various ﬁelds. For example, in animal behavior and machine learning it is well known as the exploration—exploitation
 90   trade-off, and in cognitive science it is mirrored by the free-energy principle’s account of agents balancing immediate sensory
 91  ﬁdelity against exploratory model improvement8. UEOT elevates this trade-off to a ﬁrst principle of nature: all self-evolving
 92  systems strive to simultaneously maximize “power” (Π) and knowledge (Φ). Formally, one can imagine an evolutionary vari-
 93   ational principle extremizing a combined objective—something like a weighted sum of a physical reward (analogous to proﬁt)
 94  and an informational potential—which in effect guides the object’s changes of state.
 95     Armed with these two postulates, UEOT provides what earlier frameworks lacked: a common explanatory scaffold that
 96   in principle extends from elementary particles and chemical reactions up through living cells, brains, ecosystems, and human
 97   societies. Everything from a quark to a quasar, from a bacterium to a human mind, can be viewed through the UEOT lens—as
 98  an object deﬁned by internal Ω-loops and evolving under the twin drives of Π and Φ. Phenomena that once seemed unique to
 99   different domains (metabolism in biology, learning in cognition, economic growth in society, etc.) share a deeper formal unity
100  as manifestations of the same underlying principles of topology (self-sustaining loops) and information-driven adaptation. In
101   this uniﬁed view, teleology—the appearance of purpose or goal-directedness—is not an inexplicable addition to nature, but an
102  emergent property of these twin drives acting on Ω-loop systems. In fact, UEOT formalizes teleology in scientiﬁc terms: an
103   object’s dynamics can be seen as motion through a state-space under Π/Φ optimization. From this perspective, the system’s
104  Global Optimal Direction (GOD) at any moment is the instantaneous direction in state-space that yields the steepest overall
105  improvement (the best trade-off of increased Π and Φ); and the Global Optimal Attractor (GOA) is the ultimate target state
106  of evolution—the stable end-state that maximizes the object’s long-term physical efﬁciency and informational integration.
107  These concepts, deﬁned rigorously in the UEOT framework, supply a natural measure of an object’s “intrinsic purpose”: the
108 GOA represents what the system is evolving toward (its emergent telos), and the GOD is how that purpose is enacted at each
109  moment. Teleological behavior, in other words, is nothing mystical—it is the expected outcome of a system following the
110  gradient of a dual Π/Φ potential toward an optimal attractor. By deriving concrete quantities like GOD and GOA from ﬁrst
111   principles, UEOT bridges the gap between descriptive physics and normative-sounding ideas of goals, purposes or “oughts”
112   in nature.
113      Furthermore, UEOT introduces a suite of diagnostic tools for analyzing complex systems in terms of these principles.
114  Provides quantitative measures to assess, for example, how well a subsystem’s behavior aligns with a higher-level system’s
115  objectives or how balanced an individual object’s internal drives are. In later chapters, we will see precise metrics (e.g., an
116  alignment measure ρ and a drive-balance indicator η) that allow us to diagnose when a system is near optimal harmony
117  (pursuing its purpose effectively) or when it is beset by internal conﬂicts and inefﬁciencies. In essence, UEOT offers a way to
118  measure the degree of ’purposefulness’ or adaptive ﬁt of an intricate system – something traditionally conﬁned to qualitative
119  judgment. This diagnostic capability is not only conceptually novel but has practical implications for ﬁelds from biology
120  and psychology to economics:  it makes testable the abstract notions of meaning, value, or function by anchoring them in
121  dynamical indicators of a system’s evolutionary trajectory.
122        It is important to emphasize that UEOT is put forward not as a ﬁnished theory, but as the beginning of a larger scientiﬁc
123   quest. We offer it as a foundational, axiomatic framework and research program—a strategic blueprint rather than a completed
124  ediﬁce. This paper is essentially a manifesto outlining the core ideas and a vision for a future uniﬁed science, presented with
125  both conﬁdence and humility. We are conﬁdent in the promise of these principles to illuminate the “invisible bridge” between

127  dialogue and critical evaluation, inviting scientists and thinkers across disciplines to test, reﬁne, and expand upon UEOT. By
128  engaging collectively in this effort, we hope to develop these preliminary ideas into a robust scientiﬁc framework or to discover
129  where adjustments are needed. Either outcome—validation or falsiﬁcation—will propel understanding forward, as the attempt

141 2 UEOT’s Core Ontology and Dynamical Laws

142  2.1 Topological Ontology of Objects: Existence and Classiﬁcation
143  In this section we establish the fundamental ontological premise of UEOT and classify objects accordingly. UEOT begins
144  with an axiom that redeﬁnes existence in topological terms, then builds a taxonomy of object types based on the properties of
145  these topological structures and their dynamical behavior.

146  2.2 Postulate 1: Existence as Ω-Loops
147  Postulate 1 (Topological Nature of Existence): Every entity that stably exists (every Object in UEOT) is deﬁned and sus-
148  tained by one or more closed feedback cycles in its internal structure. Each such self-sustaining cycle is termed an Ω-loop. In
149  other words, an object’s identity and persistence are secured not by its material constituents per se, but by the topological pat-
150   tern of interactions (connections) that continually regenerates the object’s state. This postulate can be summarized as topology
151   is existence: a stable object is essentially a topological loop that maintains itself.
152      Mathematically, the presence of an Ω-loop corresponds to a nontrivial cycle in the object’s state-space or interaction net-
153  work. A rigorous criterion is that the object has a nonzero ﬁrst homology group (H1 ̸= 0), indicating at least one fundamental
154  loop that cannot be continuously deformed away19. Such a loop is a topological invariant of the system. A crucial condition
155  on the Ω-loop is single-valuedness: the loop must close consistently on itself. This means that after the system’s state evolves
156  through one full cycle along the loop, all state variables return to their original values (for example, any phase-like variable
157  changes by an integer multiple of 2π so that the state is single-valued). This single-valuedness constraint ensures the feedback
158  loop truly closes without ambiguity, which underpins the object’s stability and well-deﬁned identity over time. If the Ω-loop
159   is disrupted (broken so that H1 = 0), the object loses this topological protection and cannot maintain its cohesive existence.
160  This principle is directly instantiated when a living cell “dies” because its metabolic cycle—its core Ω-loop—is broken.

161  2.2.1 Classiﬁcation of Objects via Ω-Loop Attributes
162  Given Postulate 1, we can classify objects based on attributes of their Ω-loops. Two key structural attributes are deﬁned:
163     Loop Complexity (Lc): the complexity of the object’s internal Ω-loop network. This reﬂects how intricate and layered
164  the feedback structure is—for example, a simple loop involving a few homogeneous components vs.  a highly complex,
165   hierarchical loop with many heterogeneous sub-components (such as the nested biochemical cycles in a cell or neural loops
166   in a brain). Higher loop complexity generally correlates with a greater number of interacting parts and subsystems needed to
167   sustain the loop.
168     Loop Openness (Lo): This dimension describes the degree to which an object’s Ω-loops are coupled to its environment.
169   It is not a static property, but a state-dependent variable that evolves over an object’s lifecycle. The degree of openness
170  reﬂects the object’s current evolutionary strategy and stability. We can use Type I and Type II as archetypes representing the
171  two poles of agency that emerge from this dynamic.

172        • Type I Objects (Functionally Closed Loops): This archetype represents a state of high stability and low openness.
173       The object’s Ω-loops are highly optimized and self-contained.  It interacts with the environment through highly pre-
174         dictable, low-bandwidth channels. Its persistence is due to its robust internal regulation and optimized structure, which
175       makes it less sensitive to external ﬂuctuations. This state is often the goal of an evolutionary process, corresponding to
176       an object that has reached or is near its Global Optimal Attractor (GOA).

177        • Type II Objects (Functionally Open Loops): These objects represent states characterized by high adaptability and
178       high openness.  Their Ω-loops possess numerous, highly active interfaces for exchanging energy and information
179        with the environment. Crucially, Type II existence inherently depends upon environmental coupling: from an internal
180         perspective, the observed loop appears open-ended, causing energy or information to leak at the exposed interfaces,
181        thereby breaking the closure condition. From an external perspective, however, when considering the object together
182        with its immediate environment as a uniﬁed larger-scale entity, the environmental context provides an additional loop
183         that precisely closes this gap.  Thus, at least two loops are always involved: the internal loop, which is open and
184        incomplete when viewed alone, and the external loop provided by the environment, which completes the circuit at
185        a higher scale. This functional openness enables rapid learning, exploration, and adaptability, albeit with increased
186         vulnerability to environmental perturbations.


187     The relationship between an object’s evolutionary stage and its loop openness can be understood as a dynamic lifecycle:


188      1. Emergence Phase: When a new, higher-level object emerges from the interaction of its sub-objects, it exists in a state
189        of high uncertainty and instability. During this phase, its loop openness is necessarily at its maximum. The nascent
190         object must be highly sensitive to all available information (both internal and external) to ﬁnd a viable, stable structure.
191        This is a chaotic/transient mode, rich with potential but fraught with risk.

192      2. Maturation/Optimization Phase: Once a stable structure is formed, the object begins its journey along its Global
193       Optimal Direction (GOD) towards its Global Optimal Attractor (GOA). In this phase, the object’s primary task is to
194        reﬁne its internal model and optimize its interactions.  It learns which environmental signals are important and which
195         are noise. Consequently, its loop openness will progressively decrease, becoming more selective and efﬁcient. The
196        system trades broad sensitivity for robust stability, gradually trending towards a more Type I-like operational mode as
197             it approaches its GOA.

198      3. Decay/Dissolution Phase: Due to internal wear, resource depletion, or overwhelming external shocks, the object’s core
199       Ω-loop may begin to fail. In this phase, its ability to regulate its boundaries and ﬁlter information breaks down. The
200        loop openness is then passively forced to increase again, not for exploration, but due to a loss of structural integrity.
201       The object becomes overly permeable to environmental noise, loses its internal order, and eventually dissolves back into
202           its constituent parts or a state of thermodynamic equilibrium.


203  In addition to these structural attributes, we classify an object by its dynamical mode, i.e. the qualitative pattern of its behavior
204   in time. An object’s internal Ω-loop together with its environment determine how it behaves or evolves. We deﬁne three
205  primary dynamical modes:


206        • Stable Mode (Continuous steady-state): The object’s state approaches or hovers around a ﬁxed point or steady equilib-
207        rium. Interactions are ongoing but balance out such that the object maintains a relatively constant conﬁguration over
208        time (aside from minor ﬂuctuations). This corresponds to persistence in a single stable state.

209        • Periodic Mode (Cyclic): The object undergoes regular, repeated cycles in its state. There is an oscillatory pattern (a limit
210        cycle in state-space) supported by the Ω-loop, meaning the object’s conﬁguration goes through a sequence of changes
211       and returns to its starting state in a ﬁxed period. The identity is maintained through this rhythmic renewal.

212        • Chaotic/Transient Mode (Aperiodic or complex dynamics): The object’s behavior is irregular, non-repeating, or short-
213          lived. It may exhibit chaos (sensitive, non-periodic dynamics) or exist only transiently before dissipating. In this mode,
214         the Ω-loop dynamics do not settle into a simple repeatable pattern; the trajectory in state-space is complex or decays
215          after a ﬁnite time.

216      Thus, any object in the UEOT framework can be characterized by a triplet (Lc,Lo;Mode), that is, its loop complexity, loop
217  openness (Type I vs II), and its dynamical mode (stable, periodic, or chaotic). For instance, one might describe an object
218   abstractly as (moderate complexity, closed loop; periodic) or (high complexity, open loop; chaotic) etc. This triplet provides
219  a concise proﬁle of the object’s fundamental ontological nature (what kind of feedback structure it has) and its pattern of
220   activity. Together, Postulate 1 and this classiﬁcation scheme deﬁne the core ontology of UEOT: objects are seen as topological
221  loop processes, and their variety is systematically described by how complex those loops are, how they interface with the
222  environment, and how they behave in time.

223  2.3 The Universal Law of Evolution: The Π/Φ Principle and Intrinsic Purpose
224  Having deﬁned what an object is, we now address how an object changes or evolves. UEOT posits a universal dynamical
225  law governing the evolution of all objects, encapsulated in a second fundamental postulate. This law introduces two comple-
226  mentary drives that together dictate the trajectory of an object’s state. From this principle, we will derive a natural notion of
227  purpose in the dynamics of objects.

228  2.3.1 Postulate 2: The Π/Φ Dual Drive
229  Postulate 2 (Dualistic Driver of Evolution): The evolution and behavior of every object are governed by a combined vari-
230   ational principle involving two coupled drives: a physical efﬁciency drive and an informational drive. In formal terms, the
231  dynamics of any object can be derived from an extremal (optimization) principle with two components: a proﬁt functional Π
232  and an informational potential functional Φ. This is referred to as the Π/Φ principle.
233      In essence, an object continually tries to maximize Π (achieve greater immediate payoff and efﬁciency) while minimizing
234 Φ (reduce uncertainty or ignorance). These two objectives are distinct but interlinked:
235      Proﬁt Π: This functional represents the object’s tangible performance or physical reward. Π quantiﬁes improvements in
236  energy efﬁciency, material gain, and reduction of physical costs for the object. In a simple physical context, for a Type I object
237  where informational drives are negligible, the Π functional reduces to its most basic form, corresponding to the classical ac-
238   tion’s kinetic-minus-potential energy term. This connection demonstrates how UEOT subsumes classical mechanics, viewing
239  the principle of least action as a special case of its universal optimization principle. In a biological context, Π might measure
240  net energy or resources obtained (food, reproductive success, etc.), and in an economic or organizational context it correlates
241   to ﬁnancial proﬁt or productivity gains. Generally, a higher Π means the object is doing better in terms of immediate viability
242  and efﬁcient use of resources.
243      Informational Potential Φ: This functional represents the cost of uncertainty or the potential beneﬁt of acquiring new
244   information/structure. Φ is a measure of how much the object does not know or how unadapted it is to its environment. The
245   greater the object’s uncertainty about its situation or the less optimized its internal structure, the higher Φ will be. Equivalently,
246 Φ can be thought of as an internal penalty for ignorance or disorder. This concept can be made quantitative (for example,
247  linking Φ to Fisher information or entropy measures)20, but qualitatively it means that an object is driven to explore, learn,
248  and reﬁne its internal model of the world because doing so lowers Φ. By reducing Φ, the object improves its overall prospects
249  (since knowledge can be used to secure more Π in the long run). Thus, acquiring information and improving internal order is
250   itself a fundamental drive.
251     The Π/Φ variational principle implies that evolution is a multi-dimensional optimization. An object’s trajectory is deter-
252  mined by the interplay (and often trade-off) between the Π drive and the Φ drive. Nature does not optimize a single quantity
253   like energy alone; rather, every object faces a continual balancing act between being more efﬁcient and becoming more in-
254  formed. At any moment, there may be tension between these drives (for example, exploring new possibilities might incur
255  short-term energy costs, or conserving energy might mean not gathering new information). The object’s behavior is the result
256  of a uniﬁed optimization of both: it seeks to maximize its overall viability functional that combines immediate efﬁciency and
257  long-term adaptability. We can imagine there is an effective action S[trajectory] which the object tries to extremize, with S
258  constructed from Π and Φ contributions. In concrete terms, objects evolve as if striving to improve Π while simultaneously
259  lowering Φ. This dual-drive principle is universal:  it applies to all objects irrespective of scale or domain, from particles
260  adjusting to forces, to organisms adapting in ecosystems, to organizations strategizing in markets.

261  2.3.2 GOD and GOA: The Natural Emergence of Purpose
262  The Π/Φ principle provides a built-in notion of goal-directedness for an object. We now formalize this by introducing two
263  concepts that arise from viewing the object’s evolution as a trajectory in its state-space. We treat the object’s evolution as a
264  ﬂow in a high-dimensional space of possible states or parameters. A prime example of such a ﬂow, well-established in physics,
265   is the renormalization group (RG) ﬂow, which describes how the effective state of a system changes under successive scale
266  transformations or time steps. In our universal framework, this ﬂow is driven by the Π and Φ variational dynamics—it is
267   essentially the evolutionary ﬂow of the object under its dual drives.
268     At any given state, the object experiences an impetus to change—gradients in the Π and Φ landscape pull the state in
269   certain directions. The net instantaneous direction of change can be seen as the result of these combined inﬂuences. We
270  deﬁne:

306  2.4.1 Core Mechanism: Speciﬁc Coupling to Environmental Fields
307  An object does not interact with every aspect of its environment uniformly; rather, it couples selectively to certain inﬂuences.
308 We formalize this with the concept of properties and ﬁelds. Each object O possesses a set of properties P = Pk (these could be
309  physical attributes like mass or charge, biological traits, cognitive features, etc.). The environment, in turn, can be described
310  by a set of ﬁelds F = Fk, where each Fk represents a distributed inﬂuence or gradient associated with a particular quantity
311   (for example, a gravitational ﬁeld corresponding to mass, a chemical concentration ﬁeld corresponding to a nutrient, a ﬂow of
312  information or signals corresponding to some communicative medium).
313     Speciﬁc Coupling Principle: An object O will interact signiﬁcantly with an environmental ﬁeld Fk if and only if O has the
314  corresponding property Pk that matches that ﬁeld. This principle means that coupling is selective and speciﬁc: O is effectively
315  blind to, or unaffected by, ﬁelds for which it lacks the requisite property. Conversely, if O has Pk, it will experience forces or
316  exchanges due to Fk. For example (in general terms), an object with an electric charge property responds to electromagnetic
317  ﬁelds, an organism with a certain receptor responds to the presence of a corresponding signal or nutrient in its environment,
318  and so on. If the property is absent, that ﬁeld might as well not exist for the object. This selective coupling is a universal idea
319   that includes physical forces and also generalized ﬁelds of inﬂuence in complex systems (such as economic or social ﬁelds).
320    When a coupling exists, the interaction can often be described in terms of a potential and a resulting force. The envi-
321  ronmental ﬁeld Fk creates a potential landscape Vk(x) that affects object O (here x might represent the object’s position or
322   state relative to that ﬁeld). The object experiences a force Fk proportional to the gradient of that potential: in the simplest
323   case, Fk = −∇Vk. Crucially, because of the Π/Φ principle, these ﬁelds inﬂuence the object in directions that tend to increase
324  the object’s immediate Π or reduce its Φ. In other words, the object is pulled by environmental gradients toward states that
325  promise higher proﬁt or lower risk. For instance, a resource gradient (like a higher concentration of food or energy) exerts a
326  force drawing a Type II organism toward it (increasing Π), whereas a harmful stimulus might repel the organism (avoiding Π
327   loss). Likewise, an information-rich signal in the environment can attract the attention of an object that has the apparatus to
328  perceive it, effectively pulling the object to explore or respond (reducing Φ by gaining information).
329      In UEOT, we interpret all forces—whether physical pushes and pulls or abstract inducements—under a uniﬁed scheme:
330  they are gradients in some ﬁeld to which the object is coupled, and they act to nudge the object along directions that locally

333  a way that aligns with what the object wants (in terms of the dual drives). Of course, conﬂicts can occur (e.g. a deceptive

338  2.4.2 Two Modes of Interaction: Peer-Level and Hierarchical Dynamics

339 We can distinguish two general modes of interaction involving objects: peer-level interactions, where separate objects at the
340  same level affect each other, and hierarchical interactions, which involve objects composed of sub-objects (or being part of
341   larger super-objects). UEOT provides a uniﬁed view of both modes.

342      Peer-Level Interactions: When two or more objects interact as peers, each object simply treats the others as part of its
343  environment and couples to ﬁelds or signals generated by the others. The forces or inﬂuences exchanged are thus speciﬁc
344   to each object’s needs and properties. In this mode, interactions are typically reciprocal (though not necessarily symmetric):
345  each object might exert some inﬂuence (ﬁeld) that the other can sense. The source of these interactions ultimately lies in each
346   object’s internal Π/Φ drives: for instance, one object may present an opportunity or threat to another’s proﬁt (food, compe-
347   tition) or information (uncertainty reduction, learning), and thus they will engage in dynamic interplay (such as competition,
348  cooperation, predation, communication). Peer-level forces emerge from internal needs projected outward: e.g. an animal’s
349  hunger (Π drive) creates a coupling to food sources and perhaps to other animals (prey), a company’s proﬁt motive couples
350    it to market price ﬁelds and to competitors, etc. These interactions can be complex, but they are fundamentally the result of
351  each object pursuing its own GOA in the shared environment—sometimes their trajectories align (leading to cooperation or
352  symbiosis), and sometimes they clash (leading to conﬂict or competition). UEOT’s formalism of ﬁelds and couplings handles
353  these cases as interactions of Ω-loops via the environment.

354      Hierarchical (Multi-level) Interactions: In many cases, objects are composed of smaller sub-objects (e.g. an organism
355  contains cells, an ecosystem contains organisms, an organization contains people). This creates a parent-child relationship
356  between levels. Hierarchical interaction is characterized by the inﬂuences that a higher-level object (the parent) exerts on its
357   constituent parts (the children), and vice versa. A parent object (which is itself an Ω-loop at a larger scale) will typically
358  impose an overarching order or ﬁeld that the sub-objects experience. In UEOT, this is modeled as a higher-level ﬁeld (coming
359  from the parent’s state) coupling to properties of the sub-objects. Essentially, the parent’s existence and pursuit of its GOA
360   create constraints or guiding forces on the sub-objects. For example, a multicellular organism maintains a controlled internal
361  environment (temperature, chemistry) that all its cells are subjected to; a social system enforces laws or cultural norms that
362  inﬂuence individual behavior. We can say that the parent object’s Global Optimal Attractor exerts pressure on the sub-objects:
363  the parent wants to achieve its GOA, and this manifests as shaping the conditions and rewards for the components so that
364   their behavior aligns with that goal. This is the hierarchical mode of speciﬁc coupling—a top-down inﬂuence where the
365  sub-object’s Ω-loop is not isolated, but embedded in the larger loop of the parent.

366      In a well-functioning hierarchy, the lower-level objects cooperate to fulﬁll the higher-level object’s purpose (for instance,
367   cells differentiate and work in concert for the organism’s survival; citizens contribute to the society’s stability and goals).
368  However, hierarchical conﬂict can arise if there is misalignment between a sub-object’s own optimal drive and the parent’s
369  demands. We deﬁne a hierarchical conﬂict as the situation when a child object’s GOA (the state that would be optimal for it
370   individually) is not the same as, or not compatible with, the parent object’s GOA (the optimal state of the whole). In such a
371   case, the sub-object may be driven by its internal Π/Φ to do something that contravenes the higher-level order. For example,
372  a cell might mutate and proliferate selﬁshly (its own Π drive) at the expense of the organism’s health (cancerous behavior,
373  conﬂicting with the organism’s GOA), or an individual in a social system might pursue personal proﬁt in a way that harms the
374   collective goal. When child GOA ̸= parent GOA, the speciﬁc coupling that normally ensures cohesion becomes a source of
375   tension: the parent exerts forces to try to rein in the child (e.g. immune responses, social penalties), while the child’s internal
376  drives push it in another direction. UEOT’s framework allows us to conceptualize such conﬂict in terms of competing Π/Φ
377  optimizations at different levels and can analyze conditions for stability or rupture of the hierarchy.

378      In summary, UEOT’s dynamics of interaction describe all forces and inﬂuences through the common language of speciﬁc
